newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis consider leaders corrupt as polls loom.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis consider leaders corrupt as polls loom.

text.p: Pakistanis go to the polls on February 3, but an opinion poll published on Thursday said most city-dwellers saw their leaders as hopelessly corrupt.
The respected English-language monthly Herald, based in Karachi, said 95 percent of the 1,260 people interviewed in seven cities viewed most politicians as corrupt.
The respondents were unanimous in seeing bureaucrats as the most corrupt group, while 76 percent thought army generals were more corrupt now than their counterparts 15 years ago.
Corruption is a key issue in the election campaign, with all parties promising to bring culprits to book.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
"As we stumble into Pakistan's golden jubilee year, silver linings seem to be in short supply in the enveloping gloom," Herald said in an annual issue to celebrate the anniversary.
The magazine said Pakistanis were not convinced that the corrupt would be punished.
Some 55 percent believed the corrupt would not be held accountable, against 40 percent who said they would.
A narrow 51 percent majority opposed cutting military spending, while 49 percent thought it should be slashed. But a clear 84 percent said Pakistan should keep its nuclear option.
The Herald said "anti-Indian hawks in the establishment are speaking for a minority" as its respondents voted 50 percent to 40 percent in favour of friendlier relations with India.
Fifty percent said Pakistan was unlikely to go to war with its arch-rival in the next five years, compared to 29 percent who expected such a conflict and 21 percent who had no opinion.
The magazine said a surprising one-third of respondents supported an independent Kashmir, "although a respectable majority rejects this option overall".
The poll found 34 percent in favour of Kashmiri independence and 65 percent who wanted the disputed Himalayan territory, the cause of two wars with India, to be united with Pakistan.

Officially, Islamabad wants mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite on whether to join Hindu-majority India or Islamic Pakistan. It excludes the so-called third option of a separate Kashmiri state.

According to the poll 67 percent said Pakistan's economic crisis was its own fault, while 30 percent blamed the International Monetary Fund. A 61 percent majority opposed privatisation of state-run concerns, against 37 percent who supported it.

The Herald said 72 percent felt religious parties did Pakistan more harm than good, against 25 percent who held the opposite view. Fifty-two percent thought Pakistan's founding father, Mohammad Ali Jinnah, had created it to be a religious state, while 47 percent said he had planned a modern democracy.
"Pakistanis are clearly against religious extremism," the Herald concluded, citing the 74 percent who told its pollsters that sectarian parties should be banned.
The poll said 72 percent thought Pakistan would gain more from closer ties with the Moslem world than with the West.
Thirty-two percent said they would accept restrictions on women similar to those the Islamic Taleban militia has imposed in Afghanistan, against 67 percent who said they would not.
"Of all the responses in this poll, this is perhaps the most chilling," the magazine said.
The poll said 66 percent would not allow their daughter to marry of her own free will, while 31 percent said they would.
